Agreement between null models on each interaction

Source: R/compare.R
compare_null_models.Rd

Tells, for each interaction estimated under two or more null models, whether all of them flag a deviation with the same sign, only some, none, or whether they disagree on its direction. Whether a combined effect is called an interaction depends on the null model (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025): an interaction that every plausible null model flags does not depend on that choice, whereas one flagged by only some of them needs a mechanistic hypothesis to be interpreted (Schäfer & Piggott 2018).

Usage

compare_null_models(x, null_models = NULL, alpha = 0.05)

Arguments

x

A must_interactions object from estimate_interactions(), estimated under two or more null models.

null_models

Null models to compare, among those of x. Default NULL: all of them.

alpha

Significance level applied to the adjusted p-values. Default 0.05.

Value

A data frame with one row per response, by group, sampling time, contrast set and estimand, and columns:

  • response, context and the by columns, time, set_id, order, stressors, levels, background and estimand, as in x$estimates.

  • One column per null model with the deviation it flags: "+" or "-" (adjusted p-value below alpha, with the sign of the estimate), "0" (tested, no deviation detected) or NA (not tested: not estimable, not applicable, not defined or not identifiable).

  • n_tested and n_deviating: null models tested and null models that flag a deviation.

  • agreement: "robust" (every null model tested flags a deviation, all with the same sign), "model_dependent" (some but not all of them, with the same sign), "conflicting" (deviations of opposite sign), "none" (no deviation detected under any null model) or NA (fewer than two null models tested).

  • direction: "positive" or "negative" for robust and model-dependent deviations; NA otherwise.

The attributes alpha and null_models keep the significance level and the null models compared, for report_interactions().

Details

Deviations are decided as in classify_interactions() and summary(): the adjusted p-value of each null model (adjusted within the null model, see estimate_interactions()) compared with alpha. With an equivalence margin, "0" covers both equivalent and inconclusive interactions; the verdict column of classify_interactions() tells them apart. The sign is that of the estimate on the scale of each null model, negative when the combination falls below what the null model predicts; whether that is a synergism or an antagonism depends on the direction of the single effects (see classify_interactions()). Net deviations and pure interactions are compared separately; null models that do not define an estimand (the pure interaction under DO, SAM and CA) are not tested for it.

"Robust" is relative to the null models compared, so choose those plausible for the stressors at hand. In simulated experiments generated without interaction by AD, MU, DO, SAM or CA (see "Default null model" in estimate_interactions()), requiring the six null models to agree flagged false interactions in 0.6% of the experiments on average (2.3% at most), but detected only 15% of the interactions that no mechanism explains. It is too strict a rule for detecting interactions, but it identifies those that do not depend on the null model. Model-dependent and conflicting interactions are those where the mechanistic hypothesis decides; a conflict is common when the data are compared with stress addition, which predicts larger combined effects than the other null models.

References

Madge Pimentel, I., Albini, D., Beermann, A. J., Leese, F., Macaulay, S. J., Matthaei, C. D., Orr, J. A., Piggott, J. J., & Schäfer, R. B. (2025). Hypothesis-driven research on multiple stressors: An analytical framework for stressor interactions. Ecology and Evolution, 15, e71959. doi:10.1002/ece3.71959

Schäfer, R. B., & Piggott, J. J. (2018). Advancing understanding and prediction in multiple stressor research through a mechanistic basis for null models. Global Change Biology, 24(5), 1817–1826. doi:10.1111/gcb.14073

Examples

jars <- expand.grid(
  salinity = c("ambient", "high"),
  warming = c("no", "yes"),
  replicate = 1:5,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars))
mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *
  ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.5, 1)
jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu)
design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar")
fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,
  seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU", "DO"), n_sim = 2000,
  seed = 1)
compare_null_models(est)
#>   response context time set_id order          stressors
#> 1    algae         <NA>    S01     2 salinity x warming
#>                        levels background estimand AD MU DO n_tested n_deviating
#> 1 salinity=high | warming=yes                 net  +  0  -        3           2
#>     agreement direction
#> 1 conflicting      <NA>
